```{=html}
    { text: "Arctic amplification only affects polar wildlife and sea ice — it has no documented impact on mid-latitude U.S. weather.", type: "Myth", explanation: "Multiple lines of evidence connect Arctic amplification to mid-latitude weather extremes. A warmer Arctic reduces the temperature contrast that keeps the polar jet stream tight and fast. A weaker, slower, wavier jet stream can allow polar air to plunge deeper south (polar vortex disruptions) and cause storms to stall. The February 2021 Texas freeze — where temperatures dropped below 0°F in Houston — is a prime example of Arctic amplification's reach." },
    { text: "A wavier jet stream (during Arctic amplification) means the entire United States experiences colder winters.", type: "Myth", explanation: "A wavier jet creates 'weather whiplash' — alternating extreme cold and warm regions simultaneously. When a deep trough sends Arctic air into Texas, a ridge may simultaneously bring record warmth to Alaska. So a wavier jet doesn't mean uniformly colder winters; it means more extreme contrasts — record cold in some regions at the exact same time as record warmth in others. It's redistribution, not uniform cooling." },
    { text: "New York City at approximately 41°N latitude is located within the Ferrel Cell's surface westerly wind belt.", type: "Fact", explanation: "The Ferrel Cell governs the 30°–60° latitude band, and NYC at 41°N sits squarely within it. The surface winds in the Ferrel Cell blow from the southwest (westerlies), which is why the dominant storm track across the Northeast runs from southwest to northeast. Any storm that reaches the latitude of NYC is immediately subject to the steering influence of these westerly winds." },
    { text: "As the planet warms, climate models consistently project that storm tracks will shift poleward, potentially reducing the frequency of mid-latitude storms over populated regions.", type: "Fact", explanation: "This is one of the more robust projections in climate science. As the Arctic warms faster than the tropics, the temperature gradient that drives mid-latitude circulation weakens, and the storm track density shifts toward higher latitudes. Regions currently at the center of storm belts (like the northeast U.S.) may see fewer total storms, but those that do occur may be more intense due to increased atmospheric moisture — the 'fewer but stronger' pattern already visible in several datasets." }
  ];
  var idx = 0, score = 0, answered = 0, cardAnswered = false;
  function updateCard() {
    if (idx >= cards.length) {
      document.getElementById('spmf-card').style.display = 'none';
      document.getElementById('spmf-myth').style.display = 'none';
      document.getElementById('spmf-fact').style.display = 'none';
      document.getElementById('spmf-feedback').style.display = 'none';
      document.getElementById('spmf-next').style.display = 'none';
      document.getElementById('spmf-done').style.display = 'block';
      document.getElementById('spmf-final').textContent = score;
      return;
    }
    document.getElementById('spmf-card').textContent = cards[idx].text;
    document.getElementById('spmf-progress').textContent = 'Card ' + (idx + 1) + ' of ' + cards.length;
    document.getElementById('spmf-feedback').style.display = 'none';
    document.getElementById('spmf-next').style.display = 'none';
    document.getElementById('spmf-myth').disabled = false;
    document.getElementById('spmf-fact').disabled = false;
    document.getElementById('spmf-myth').style.opacity = '1';
    document.getElementById('spmf-fact').style.opacity = '1';
    cardAnswered = false;
  }
  window.spmfAnswer = function(choice) {
    if (cardAnswered) return;
    cardAnswered = true;
    answered++;
    var card = cards[idx];
    var correct = (choice === card.type);
    if (correct) score++;
    document.getElementById('spmf-score').textContent = score;
    document.getElementById('spmf-total').textContent = answered;
    var fb = document.getElementById('spmf-feedback');
    fb.style.display = 'block';
    fb.style.background = correct ? 'rgba(0,184,148,0.2)' : 'rgba(214,48,49,0.2)';
    fb.style.border = '1px solid ' + (correct ? '#00b894' : '#e17055');
    fb.innerHTML = '<strong>' + (correct ? '✅ Correct! ' : '❌ That\'s a ' + card.type + '! ') + '</strong>' + card.explanation;
    document.getElementById('spmf-myth').disabled = true;
    document.getElementById('spmf-fact').disabled = true;
    document.getElementById('spmf-myth').style.opacity = (choice === 'Myth') ? '1' : '0.5';
    document.getElementById('spmf-fact').style.opacity = (choice === 'Fact') ? '1' : '0.5';
    document.getElementById('spmf-next').style.display = 'block';
  };
  window.spmfNext = function() { idx++; updateCard(); };
  window.spmfRestart = function() {
    idx = 0; score = 0; answered = 0;
    document.getElementById('spmf-card').style.display = 'flex';
    document.getElementById('spmf-myth').style.display = 'block';
    document.getElementById('spmf-fact').style.display = 'block';
    document.getElementById('spmf-done').style.display = 'none';
    document.getElementById('spmf-score').textContent = '0';
    document.getElementById('spmf-total').textContent = '0';
    updateCard();
  };
  updateCard();
})();
</script>
```

# Summary: Key Takeaways

| Concept | Key Idea |
|---------|----------|
| **Uneven heating** | Equator gets more solar energy → drives convection cells |
| **Convection cells** | Hadley, Ferrel, Polar cells redistribute heat globally |
| **Coriolis effect** | Earth's rotation deflects winds → creates prevailing wind patterns |
| **Westerlies** | Dominant winds in 30°–60° latitude → steer storms SW → NE |
| **Jet stream** | Fast upper-level winds at cell boundaries → storm "highway" |
| **Arctic amplification** | Reduced gradient → wavier jet stream → storms may stall or shift |
| **Storm tracks** | Both hurricanes and blizzards are steered by the same global winds |

**Next up:** We'll investigate **how hurricanes form** and why they only occur during certain months. 🌀
